name: Herbst / twin-block functional appliance

lead: The Herbst (fixed) and Twin Block (removable) are functional appliances that hold the lower jaw forward in growing children and teenagers with a Class II overbite. The payoff is a corrected bite and a stronger chin and side profile; in looksmaxxing forums they are discussed as a way to advance a small or recessed lower jaw.

The appliance postures the lower jaw forward. Trials and meta-analyses report a modest average gain in lower-jaw length, around 1.5 to 2 mm or more versus controls, together with tooth movement. A review found about two-thirds of samples showed more than 2 mm of extra lengthening, with larger effects during puberty. How much is skeletal rather than dental remains debated.

paras: An orthodontist fits the Herbst, fixed with telescoping rods, or the Twin Block, a removable pair of acrylic plates, during the growth period, typically for months before further orthodontic treatment.

Reported effects include early soreness and chewing difficulty, speech changes with removable plates, and forward tilting of lower front teeth. A 2022 meta-analysis did not support forum claims that they recess the upper jaw.

angle.text: Herbst and Twin Block appliances hold the lower jaw forward in growing teens with an overbite, adding modest lower-jaw length and improving the side profile. Research is mostly in children; adult aesthetic use and home-made versions are not covered.

lead: The Herbst appliance and the Twin Block appliance are orthodontic devices known as functional appliances. They are used in growing children and adolescents with a Class II malocclusion, in which the upper front teeth sit forward of the lower ones and the lower jaw is often small or set back relative to the upper jaw. The Herbst is fixed to the teeth and holds the lower jaw forward through telescoping rods, while the Twin Block is a removable pair of acrylic plates that guide the lower jaw forward when the patient bites together. [1][2]

Systematic reviews generally report that functional appliances correct overjet and molar relationship in growing patients, with a mix of tooth movement and skeletal change. A review of mandibular changes found that about two-thirds of the studied samples showed more than 2 mm of supplementary lower-jaw lengthening compared with untreated controls, with larger effects when treatment coincided with the pubertal growth period. [3] A meta-analysis comparing the two appliances reported slightly greater mandibular body lengthening with the Herbst. [1] Whether the change is lasting and how much of it is skeletal rather than dental remains debated in the orthodontic literature. [3][3]

In looksmaxxing communities the devices are discussed as a way to advance a 'recessed' lower jaw in teenagers, alongside surgery, fillers and over-the-counter mouthguards. Posters ask whether the appliances can be obtained cheaply or reproduced at home, and some threads claim that orthodontic appliances can hold back upper-jaw growth. [4][5][6]

paras: The Herbst appliance is a fixed device: a metal framework is attached to the upper molars and lower premolars, and a telescoping rod and tube on each side lets the patient open and close while keeping the lower jaw in a forward position. It does not rely on the patient wearing it, and treatment is commonly described as lasting several months. [7]

The Twin Block consists of upper and lower acrylic plates with interlocking inclined planes. When the patient closes, the planes guide the lower jaw forward. It is removable, so results depend partly on the patient wearing it.  Variants include mini-implant-supported and clear versions that have been tested in recent randomised trials.
Both appliances belong to a wider family that includes the Forsus fatigue resistance device and Class II elastics, which are also used to correct a Class II relationship. [2]

Functional appliances hold the lower jaw in a forward posture. Orthodontists describe the resulting change as a combination of tooth movement (upper teeth tipped back, lower teeth tipped forward), alveolar adaptation, and possible additional lower-jaw growth or remodelling at the joint. Early cephalometric studies of the Herbst reported correction of the bite through both dental and skeletal changes. [8][9] MRI and radiographic work has examined how the temporomandibular joint remodels during Herbst treatment. [10]

A systematic review of 22 controlled studies of functional appliances found that two-thirds of the samples showed a clinically relevant extra mandibular elongation of more than 2 mm versus untreated controls, and that the effect appeared larger when treatment was timed around the pubertal growth peak. Study quality ranged from low to medium or high. [3]

A UK multicentre randomised trial of 174 children aged 8 to 10 with Class II Division 1 malocclusion compared early Twin Block treatment with no treatment over 15 months. [11] A separate randomised trial compared the Herbst and the Twin Block directly. [12] A 2024 meta-analysis of 12 studies with 574 patients found greater mandibular body length increase and more lower-incisor proclination with the Herbst than with the Twin Block. [1]

A 2022 meta-analysis of nine studies (298 patients) found that Herbst and Forsus appliances produced similar changes to Class II elastics on most measures, with Herbst showing about 1.5 mm more mandibular length and 1.6 mm more ramus height. [2] A Cochrane review of early versus late treatment of prominent upper front teeth in children covers related orthodontic approaches.

Recent randomised trials have tested a mini-implant-supported Twin Block against the conventional version, a modified clear Twin Block, and speech effects of a clear versus conventional Twin Block.  Work on soft-tissue profile change after functional therapy and on head and cervical posture after Twin Block or Bionator treatment has also been published.  A 2025 meta-analysis examined functional clear aligners for Class II correction in growing patients against approaches that included the Twin Block.  These studies were conducted in children and adolescents for medical orthodontic indications. No studies examined the appliances as a facial-aesthetic procedure in adults.

Reported effects of fixed functional appliances include early discomfort and difficulty chewing, and tooth movement such as lower-incisor proclination, which meta-analyses record as an outcome. [7][1] Removable appliances can affect speech during the adjustment period, which a randomised trial has measured.  Because the appliances are used in growing patients under orthodontic supervision, the documented effects in the literature relate to that setting.

Emil Herbst developed the appliance in the early 1900s according to current encyclopedic accounts, and an 1886 editorial in The Dental Register already refers to Herbst's method. [13][7] It fell out of wide use and was reintroduced by Hans Pancherz, whose cephalometric studies from 1979 onward helped establish its modern use. [7][8][9] The Twin Block technique is documented in a 1988 article in the American Journal of Orthodontics and Dentofacial Orthopedics.

On looksmax.org, users in their mid-teens ask whether a Herbst can be obtained when cost is a barrier, and whether a home-made alternative exists. One reply recommends a commercial mouthguard-type device as a cheaper option, and the original poster expresses doubt about the seller's website. [5] Other threads ask whether the Herbst or Forsus can be used without an overbite, whether it recesses the upper jaw, and whether functional appliances affect the lower third of the face. [6][14][15] One thread asserts that orthodontists using Herbst appliances and rubber bands stunt upper-jaw growth. [4]
